$comment: Kaana's MEASURED deployment inventory. Every upstream model id below was read from a live provider API with that account's own key. Nothing here is copied from documentation.

It holds no Oxy-owned concept — no account, application, credential, price or commercial permission. The provider API keys are not here and never will be: a slug resolves to an adapter, an address and a key pool in cmd/kaana, from the process environment.

PUBLISHER IS WHO RELEASED THE WEIGHTS, NEVER WHO SERVES THEM. `openai/gpt-oss-120b` is served BY Cerebras, which is why `provider` says cerebras and the reference does not. OpenRouter's ids already carry the releasing publisher in that same slot, which is why they transcribe directly. The one placeholder is `stealth/`, which OpenRouter uses for a release whose publisher is undisclosed; when it is disclosed the id changes upstream too, so the reference changes with it and nothing here is a guess about who made it.

THE REVISION LABEL IS OXY'S OBSERVATION, NOT THE PUBLISHER'S RELEASE. Neither provider exposes a publisher revision handle. Cerebras's ids are bare aliases with `created: 0`. OpenRouter publishes `created`, but that is the date OpenRouter listed the model; it also publishes a `canonical_slug`, and 201 of the 421 entries carry a dated one — which is OpenRouter's listing identity, not a revision the publisher issued, and is absent from the rest. Adopting it would put two pin schemes in one file, and a file with two pin schemes cannot express one set of weights served by two providers. So the pin says exactly what is known: the date Oxy observed the alias.

ONE SET OF WEIGHTS IS ONE REFERENCE, EVEN ACROSS PROVIDERS AND OBSERVATION DATES. `openai/gpt-oss-120b` is served by both providers here and was observed on two different days. It is declared ONCE, under the label of the FIRST observation, with two deployments — because two observations of one model are not two revisions, and the loader refuses a model line with two current revisions rather than picking one. Each deployment id still records the day that deployment was observed. Cerebras is declared first because it was already the declared route and nothing measured on 2026-08-23 displaces it; this is not a price decision, because Cerebras publishes no price through its API.

`GET https://api.cerebras.ai/v1/models` returned exactly these two and nothing else; `GET /v1/models/<id>` answered 200 for both while every id outside the list answered 404 `model_not_found`. On that day the account answered 402 `payment_required` (`param: quota`) to every chat completion, on both models, while the same key answered 200 on the model endpoints — the key is valid and the account cannot be billed. The 402 arrives after model validation, which is what confirms the two ids are real for this account. Inference starts working when the Cerebras account can be billed; nothing in this file changes then.

`GET https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models` returned 421 entries. 340 are declared below, as 340 deployments over 329 references. The 81 that are not declared were excluded for three measured reasons, not skipped:

EXCLUDED, 6 ROUTERS (openrouter/auto-beta, openrouter/fusion, openrouter/pareto-code, openrouter/free, openrouter/bodybuilder, openrouter/auto). Five say in their own description that they choose a different model per request — routed to one of dozens, selected at random from the free models, ranked off a tiered shortlist. That is precisely the substitution Kaana refuses to make, and declaring one would hand the choice of model to the provider behind a reference that claims to name it. All six also put the SERVING provider in the publisher slot, which the rule above forbids.

EXCLUDED, 13 MOVING ALIASES (the twelve `~<publisher>/…-latest` ids, plus `openai/gpt-chat-latest`). Their descriptions state the behaviour outright — "always redirects to the latest GLM model from Z.ai", "always resolves to the latest Instant chat model used in ChatGPT". The weights behind the id change without the id changing, so pinning one would produce a reference that promises immutability and does not have it. The dated releases they point at are declared individually and can be pinned honestly.

EXCLUDED, 62 ENDPOINT VARIANTS (61 `:batch`, 1 `:thinking`). These are not other weights, they are another way of being served — asynchronous batch at roughly half price, and an extended-reasoning mode. `<publisher>/<model>@<revision>` has no slot for a delivery mode, so declaring them would take one of two bad shapes: inventing a model name no publisher released (`openai/gpt-5-batch`), or folding them into the base reference, where a failover would answer a streaming request from a batch endpoint. Both are worse than the gap. If Kaana ever gains a first-class notion of delivery mode, they belong to it and not to a reference.

`GET https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/models` returned 13. SEVEN are declared; the other six were excluded on what Groq itself publishes, not on judgement. Groq is the only provider here that states `input_modalities`/`output_modalities` per model, so the cut is measured: two Orpheus voices output `speech` and two Whisper models output `transcription` from `audio` input, and none of the four is reachable through a chat-completions adapter — declaring them would be four routes that answer an error. `groq/compound` and `groq/compound-mini` are `owned_by: Groq`, which would put the SERVING provider in the publisher slot; that is refused by the same rule the gate asserts, without needing any claim about what they do internally.

GROQ'S PUBLISHER SLUGS COME FROM ITS OWN `owned_by` FIELD, MAPPED ONTO THE SLUG THIS FILE ALREADY USES. `owned_by: OpenAI` on `openai/gpt-oss-120b` is why Groq joins Cerebras and OpenRouter on ONE reference instead of minting a third. `owned_by: Meta` maps to `meta-llama`, the slug the eight Llama-family lines already carry (OpenRouter's `meta/*` entries are the Muse family, so that split is by model family and not an inconsistency to resolve here). `owned_by: Alibaba Cloud` maps to `qwen`, and `owned_by: SDAIA` mints `sdaia`, which no other provider in this file serves. The build FAILS rather than guesses if an `owned_by` has no decided slug, or if a namespaced id and its `owned_by` disagree.

`GET https://api.x.ai/v1/models` returned 12, which mixes model types. `GET /v1/language-models` returns the SEVEN that are chat-servable, and those are what is declared; the three image-generation models and the two video models are not, for the same reason the Groq voices are not. Each of the seven reports `input_modalities: [text, image]`, `output_modalities: [text]` and its own `fingerprint`, so `grok-4.20-multi-agent-0309` is declared like the rest: it has distinct weights and nothing xAI publishes says it resolves to another model.

XAI'S ALIASES ARE EXCLUDED BY CONSTRUCTION, NOT BY A FILTER. Each entry carries an `aliases` array — `grok-4.20-beta-latest`, `grok-4.20-non-reasoning-latest` and a dozen more — while the `id` field holds the dated canonical (`grok-4.20-0309-reasoning`). Reading `id` therefore takes the pinnable name and leaves every moving one behind, which is why no `-latest` filter appears in the generator for this provider.

DECLARATION ORDER ACROSS PROVIDERS IS THE PROVIDER ORDER, AND IT IS NOT A PRICE CLAIM. Within one provider the endpoints of a reference are ordered by that provider's own published prompt price. ACROSS providers there is no comparable number here: Cerebras publishes no price at all, and xAI's `prompt_text_token_price` is an integer in an undocumented unit that cannot be compared with OpenRouter's dollars-per-token without inventing a conversion. So the order is `cerebras, groq, xai, openrouter` — the operators that run the model ahead of the reseller — declared as a POLICY and not as a measurement. Production reports `costMeasured: false`; whoever loads a rate card should revisit this deliberately.

EIGHT REFERENCES ARE NOW SERVED BY MORE THAN ONE PROVIDER, which is the failover set the schema exists to express — `openai/gpt-oss-120b` by three. Failover is still off by default, so each resolves to its first declared deployment and the rest are inert until a routing policy authorises them.

FREE IS DECLARED FIRST, AND THAT ORDERING IS THE WHOLE MECHANISM. 11 references carry both a `:free` endpoint and a paid one. Within every reference the endpoints are ordered by prompt price ascending, so the free endpoint is declared FIRST in all 11. Failover is off by default, so a reference resolves to the deployment declared first and nowhere else: today those 11 resolve to the free endpoint and the paid sibling is inert. This is an ORDERING, NOT A BUDGET — it cannot cap spend, count tokens or ration a key, and it does not fall back to the paid endpoint when the free one is rate-limited. Rationing is key-pool policy in cmd/kaana; nothing in an inventory can do it.

THE FREE AND PAID SIBLINGS DO NOT ACCEPT THE SAME CONTEXT, AND FAILOVER IS NOW ON, SO HERE IS EXACTLY WHERE THAT COSTS SOMETHING. Of the nine references carrying both endpoints, SEVEN are safe in the direction failover travels: the paid sibling admits the same context as the free one or more, so anything that fitted the free endpoint fits the paid one. TWO are not, and only above a specific size: `nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b` (free 1,000,000, paid 512,288) and `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning` (free 1,000,000, paid 262,144). A request larger than the paid limit that is throttled on the free endpoint fails over and is then refused for LENGTH — the caller sees `context_length_exceeded`, which is non-retryable by the contract, where without failover they would have seen a retryable throttle. That is the whole cost: two references, requests above 512,288 and 262,144 tokens, and a less useful error code rather than a wrong answer. Kaana never substitutes a different model, so nothing here can return the wrong weights.

THE OPENROUTER ROUTES WERE PROBED, AND THE ACCOUNT'S OWN CREDIT ENDPOINT IS NOT A GUIDE TO THEM. `GET /api/v1/credits` answers `total_credits: 0, total_usage: 0` and `GET /api/v1/auth/key` says `is_free_tier: true` — and a PAID model nevertheless completed, returned content, and reported `cost: 0.000080255`, after which both figures were still zero. So the paid routes ARE servable today and that endpoint does not track them. An earlier revision of this file said the paid remainder would answer a payment error until the account was funded; a real completion falsified it.

THIRTEEN OF THE EIGHTEEN `:free` ENDPOINTS ANSWERED 200 ON A REAL COMPLETION. Three answered 429 whose upstream body says `temporarily rate-limited upstream. Please retry shortly` — transient, per-model, and upstream rather than OpenRouter's own throttle. Because failover is off by default, a reference whose free endpoint is declared first does NOT fall through to its paid sibling while that lasts; it fails. That is the cost of the free-first ordering, stated rather than discovered.

TWO `:free` ENDPOINTS ARE REFUSED PERMANENTLY AND ARE NOT DECLARED: `thinkingmachines/inkling:free` and `inkling-small:free` answer 403 `only available on agentic harnesses`, which is a product gate and not a rate limit — no retry reaches them. They appear in `GET /models` exactly like every servable id, so nothing short of a real completion distinguishes them, which is why they were probed. Their PAID siblings are declared and are now each reference's only endpoint.

THIS FILE IS NOT WHAT PRODUCTION SERVES. The Dockerfile ships no inventory — baking one would freeze its `issuedAt` — so a deployment reads what `relay-publisher` writes to the mounted volume, not this. And the publisher would today discover NOTHING for OpenRouter: `configs/model-attribution.json` has no `openrouter` entry, and a model nobody attributed is dropped and named, never guessed. So this is the measured content a publisher can re-issue, and getting it served is three separate things — attribution, a credential, and `RELAY_PROVIDERS` naming the slug.

DECLARING A PROVIDER HERE IS A BOOT REQUIREMENT. The server refuses to start if a provider this file routes to has no adapter configured, rather than discovering it on a customer request. So `openrouter` must be named in RELAY_PROVIDERS with a protocol and a base URL before this snapshot is published, or the process will not come up.

NO REGION, EITHER PROVIDER. Neither publishes a region for these endpoints, so none is declared. An invented one would not stay decorative: `allowedRegions`/`deniedRegions` match on exact strings, so a residency policy would later admit or refuse these routes on a value nobody measured.

STALENESS IS MEASURED FROM `issuedAt`, AND THIS ONE IS FROZEN AT COMMIT. A checked-in file is stale within RELAY_INVENTORY_MAX_AGE (default 1h) of the instant below, after which PINNED references are still served and UNPINNED ones are refused. So this is the content of a snapshot, not a snapshot a deployment can live on: whatever publishes into /etc/relay must re-issue it with a fresh `issuedAt` on a cadence shorter than the horizon, even when not one byte of it has changed.
